name: Edo Tokyo yasai (Edo-Tokyo heritage vegetables)
text: A designation by JA Tokyo Chuokai for Tokyo vegetables that carry on the food culture of the Edo period. The definition covers vegetables derived from landraces or traditional cultivation methods whose seed, until the mid-Showa era, was mostly self-saved or bought from nearby seed merchants. 52 kinds were registered as of October 2024. Wikipedia adds that some varieties came from seed brought to Edo by daimyo on sankin-kotai and were adapted to Edo conditions.
flavor: Used as a quality label on menus and at markets; signals old local cultivars, not a taste profile.
use: Cited on menus and sourcing sheets to name Tokyo landraces such as Nerima daikon, Kameido daikon, Terajima nasu and Goseki bansei komatsuna.
craft: The term is an association registry, not a legal standard. When buying, check which cultivar is meant (for example the traditional komatsuna cultivars versus modern commercial ones), because plain komatsuna sold in Tokyo is mostly improved varieties.
src: JA Tokyo Aoba: Edo Tokyo yasai list

name: Nerima daikon
text: White-neck daikon grown in Nerima since the Genroku era of the Edo period and prosperous until early Showa. The 1933 (Showa 8) great drought and an outbreak of mosaic disease hit it hard. Roots reach about 70-100 cm, thin at the neck and tip and thick in the middle, with strong pungency. Legend ties its start to the 5th shogun Tsunayoshi convalescing near Nerima.
flavor: Strongly pungent, firm, long and fibrous root.
use: Today the type grown is the Nerima shirihoso (thin-tailed) daikon, suited to takuan pickling. Hard to pull: said to need 3-5 times the force of an ordinary daikon, hence the Nerima daikon pulling contest held with Nerima Ward.
craft: Pungency and length make it a pickling daikon rather than a raw-salad one; judge for a straight, thin-tailed root suited to sun-drying for takuan.
src: JA Tokyo Aoba: Edo Tokyo yasai list

name: Traditional komatsuna (Goseki bansei and Jonan komatsuna)
ja: 伝統小松菜(後関晩生・城南小松菜)
text: Komatsuna is tied by tradition to Komatsugawa in present Edogawa Ward; the popular story says shogun Yoshimune liked the greens eaten there and named them after the place, which is a legend rather than documented history. Edo Tokyo yasai komatsuna has two cultivars: Goseki bansei komatsuna (Edogawa and western Tokyo) and Jonan komatsuna, a fixed variety of Setagaya and Ota. Most komatsuna now sold is improved varieties; the old types are disappearing from fields.
flavor: Edogawa sources credit sea-breeze minerals in the soil with added sweetness.
craft: If a menu says traditional komatsuna, ask which of the two cultivars; the Edogawa Ward page explains sweetness through soil minerals, a claim that comes from the ward, not a trial.

name: Kameido daikon
text: Small daikon grown since the Edo period around Kameido Katori Shrine and named after the place in early Taisho. The root is short, tapering to a wedge-shaped point, and was formerly called otafuku or okame daikon. Sources disagree on size: about 30 cm in one, about 15 cm in another. Production has moved to the Takasago area; both root and leaves were eaten as asazuke.
flavor: Tender; leaf and root eaten together.
use: Asazuke using root and leaves together.
craft: Because root length is reported inconsistently, specify size when ordering. The leaves are part of the product; do not buy it topped.

name: Terajima nasu
text: Small eggplant raised in Terajima village, around present Higashi-Mukojima in Sumida Ward. Small in size but described as strongly flavored. It once died out and has been revived in recent years by volunteers.
flavor: Small fruit with pronounced eggplant flavor.
use: Edo Tokyo yasai eggplant used as a regional ingredient.
craft: The sources seen give no detail on skin, seed or cooking behavior; verify cultivar and grower with the revival group before listing it by name.
src: JA Tokyo Aoba: Edo Tokyo yasai list

name: Noraboh-na
text: Cold-hardy brassica grown around Tokyo, Kanagawa and Saitama. It is said to have helped feed Edo in famine because breaking off the flower stalk makes it throw new shoots again, a sign of strong vitality. Boiled, it gives a bright green color and sweetness.
use: Eaten as boiled greens and flower stalks.
craft: Harvest by snapping the flower stalks; the plant re-sprouts, so a single plant gives repeated picking. Do not overboil, since color is its selling point.

name: Miura daikon
text: White-neck daikon of the Miura Peninsula, grown since the Edo period (around 1812) and formally named Miura daikon in 1925 (Taisho 14). Flesh is dense, tender and sweet and resists falling apart in cooking.
craft: Chosen for long simmering because it holds its shape; judge for dense, even flesh.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Kanagawa

name: Dadachamame (Tsuruoka brown-hair edamame)
text: Tsuruoka landrace edamame handed down since the Edo period, of the brown-hair (chamoke) type. Pods carry brown down and often hold two beans. It is reported to contain more alanine and other free amino acids, the sweet and umami components, than ordinary varieties. The name comes from the Shonai dialect for father, with a lord-asking-whose-father story; another version says the head of household ate first. Growers' groups narrow the strains to eight, while another source lists six lines.
use: Boiled in the pod in summer and eaten freshly.
craft: The number of strains varies by source (6 or 8), so name the strain when it matters. Grown in a limited area; eat fresh after harvest.

name: Akane horenso (red-root spinach of Murayama)
text: Landrace spinach of the Murayama region of Yamagata, with red root and leaf bases. Cold-hardy and resistant to snow breakage. Soft, low in aku and strongly sweet. It is said that early in Showa, Yamagata City farmers selected deeper-red plants to develop it.
craft: Retail-based sources only; the red base is the quality mark, and a deep-red root indicates the selection.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Yamagata

name: Tonaijima cucumber
text: Shonai landrace cucumber from the Tonaijima district of Tsuruoka. Skin is half white and half green. Used mostly for pickles and pickled slices. A legend says Kobo Daishi ate it to ease thirst on the way to Dewa Sanzan.
craft: Information comes from local retailers rather than primary sources; the bicolor skin is the identifying trait.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Yamagata

name: Yukina (snow greens of Yonezawa)
text: A vegetable raised under snow in Yonezawa, mainly made into fusube-zuke. Its origin is traced to Uesugi Yozan, lord of Yonezawa, who encouraged growing it to secure fresh greens in snow country.
flavor: Pickled, with the character of a winter green.
craft: Sources are retail pages; the sources give no cultivation steps.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Yamagata

name: Juzen nasu
text: Niigata kinchaku (purse-shaped) eggplant with thin deep-navy skin and firm yet tender flesh with mild sweetness. Origin accounts differ: one says it was bred at the former Juzen village (Gosen) by crossing Senshu mizunasu with a native type, then improved into Kuro-juzen, which a Sanjo seed merchant spread; Nagaoka calls it nashi-nasu. Another source says an early Wakayama eggplant was brought to Muikamachi in the 1897-1906 range (Meiji 30s). Shipping mid-June to late September.
flavor: Thin skin, firm yet tender flesh, mild sweetness.
use: Mostly asazuke; also the well-known Juzen nasu-zuke.
craft: Most volume today is F1 seed-company varieties, so ask whether a plain juzen is the old type. Best in the June to September shipping window.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Niigata

name: Kagura nanban
text: Niigata chili pepper whose fruit shapes run round, bell-like or shishito-like, turning from green to red as it ripens. The heat is concentrated in the seeds and the tissue around them. Grown in Nagaoka, Uonuma, Joetsu and Ojiya.
flavor: Mild flesh with heat concentrated at the seeds.
craft: Remove seeds and surrounding pith to temper the heat; leave them in for pungency.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Niigata

name: Nagaoka kinchaku nasu (Nakajima kinchaku)
text: Kinchaku eggplant certified as a Nagaoka yasai by the Nagaoka Yasai Brand Association. Nakajima kinchaku is said to trace to seed brought from Kameda-machi in the Meiji 40s (1907-1916); the name comes from several ridges running from the calyx. Some hold Nakajima kinchaku and Nagaoka kinchaku are the same thing.
use: Usually steamed whole as fukashi nasu.
craft: Steaming rather than frying is the standard handling. Check whether the supplier means the certified Nagaoka type.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Niigata

name: Kintoki-sou
text: Kaga yasai with leaves of vivid red-purple and a distinctive sticky texture. Kanazawa certifies 15 Kaga yasai items, defined as vegetables grown since before 1945 and still grown in Kanazawa.
flavor: Mucilaginous, with a distinctive slippery texture.
craft: Its color is the point; keep cooking short for dressed dishes.
src: Kanazawa City: what is Kaga yasai

name: Uchiki akagawa amaguri kabocha
ja: 打木赤皮甘栗かぼちゃ
text: Vermilion kabocha with soft skin and moist flesh. Said to have been bred by Inoue Gensuke, a farmer in Aichi, and improved by Matsumoto Saichiro. The flesh is soft but resists collapse. Production fell, and it is treated as a traditional vegetable with seed preservation.
flavor: Moist, soft flesh, chestnut-like sweetness suggested by the name.
craft: Chosen for simmering because it holds shape; the skin is eaten.
src: Maruka Ishikawa Chuo Seika: Kaga yasai

name: Futatsuka karashina
text: Kaga yasai mustard green with wasabi-like pungency and a nose-piercing aroma, used in pickles. Cultivation once declined; seed is now preserved.
craft: Sources give no further technique; use the heat fresh.
src: Maruka Ishikawa Chuo Seika: Kaga yasai

name: Nozawana
text: Leaf vegetable named after Nozawa Onsen village. A priest of Kenmeiji is said to have brought Tennoji turnip seed from Kyoto around the Horeki era (1756); the plant grew large leaves instead of a large root and was adopted. Its pickles are counted among Japan's three major pickled greens.
craft: Origin is a temple tradition; the large leaf rather than a bulbous root is the defining trait.

name: Inekoki-na
text: Pickling green from the Inekoki area of Matsumoto, said to have come from the Hida region, and once counted among the prefecture's three major pickling greens. Leaves are fibrous and firm but with a good bite, used for green and turnip pickles.
craft: The tough leaf suits long pickling.
src: Matsumoto City: Shinshu Matsumoto traditional vegetables

name: Hodaira kabu
text: Turnip grown for a long time in the Nagawa area of Matsumoto. The root is conical with vivid red skin, sweet with little pungency. In sweet-vinegar pickle the skin pigment bleeds into the brine and turns it pink.
craft: Pickling releases the red skin color, so brine turns pink.
src: Matsumoto City: Shinshu Matsumoto traditional vegetables

name: Habiro-na
text: Pickling green originating in Ina City and one of the Shinshu three major pickling greens with nozawana and inekoki-na. Leaves suit light pickles, while locals especially value the root, pickled in sake lees and miso.
flavor: Leaf for light pickles; root prized.
use: Light leaf pickles; root pickled in sake lees and miso.
craft: Use both leaf and root, treating each differently.

name: Shinshu dento yasai certification
ja: 信州伝統野菜認定制度
text: Nagano Prefecture's certification, launched in 1991, under which a committee checks standards for each variety. There are also separate certifications for growers who meet production standards and for processed foods made by traditional methods. Counts differ by source: Wikipedia cites 71 items as of May 2015, while a more recent article cites 79 or 85.
use: Label for Nagano landraces such as nozawana, habiro-na, inekoki-na and hodaira kabu.
craft: Check the official prefectural list for the current count.

name: Gokayama kabu
text: Landrace turnip of Gokayama, said to have been brought by fleeing Heike warriors. It was grown in slash-and-burn farming and seed was saved by each farm, so color and shape differ from farm to farm.
craft: Because seed is saved by each household, expect variation in color and shape.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Toyama

name: Nyuzen jumbo watermelon
text: Toyama watermelon averaging 15-18 kg, with heavy ones reaching 30 kg. In season late July to early August, long oval like a rugby ball, with dark skin and clear stripes. Registered as a geographical indication in December 2017, the first GI product of Toyama Prefecture.
flavor: Large oblong watermelon with dark, striped rind.
craft: The GI registration documents describe the standards; check the stripe clarity and shape listed there.

name: Yoshikawa nasu
text: Round eggplant grown in the former Yoshikawa village in Sabae, revived as a traditional vegetable. Flesh is dense and soft and pairs well with oil, so it suits dengaku and agebitashi.
craft: Oil cooking is the recommended handling.

name: Yadabe negi
text: Negi of the Yadabe district of Obama. A distinctive growing method softens the white part, the base bends like a fishhook, and sweetness is strong.
craft: The bent base reflects its special cultivation.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Fukui

name: Kochi akakabura
text: Landrace red turnip of the Miyama area of Fukui City, with vivid red-purple color and firm flesh. Counted among the Fukui Hyakusai Yasai. Sources write the place as Miyama-cho or Miyama district.
craft: Sources give no technique.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Fukui

name: Nanbu futo negi
text: Landrace negi of Nanbu town, Aomori, revived from near extinction when students of a prefectural agricultural high school took over the seed. Sweet and the leaves are edible; the white part can exceed 3 cm in diameter. Because it has not been repeatedly crossed it is weak to disease and hard to grow.
craft: Disease susceptibility makes it hard to grow.

name: Junsai (Akita Moritake)
text: Perennial water plant whose young leaves and stalks, translucent and slimy, rise from the rhizome and are eaten. In Akita it moved from natural ponds in the Moritake area to cultivation in converted paddy fields and is presented as Japan's top producing area.
craft: Sources do not give harvest detail.

name: Keitoku onion (Aizu)
text: Onion grown in the Aizu region of Fukushima, listed among Aizu traditional vegetables alongside Aizu maru nasu. Known as soft with strong sweetness.
craft: Sources give no further detail.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Fukushima

name: Aizu koiku kabocha
text: Aizu kabocha that is small and flat in shape, strongly sweet, with floury flesh that does not collapse in cooking.
craft: Floury flesh holds shape.
src: Japan Traditional Vegetable Promotion Assoc.: Fukushima

name: Sapporoki onion
text: Landrace yellow onion born in Meiji-era Sapporo. Onion cultivation in Japan is said to have started in 1871 with imported seed trialed at the Sapporo Kaitakushi garden; one theory says Yellow Globe Danvers was the base. Small but thick-fleshed, sweet and pungent raw, losing pungency when cooked. Sugar is given as 13 degrees (Slow Food Japan) or 12 degrees in other articles. Weak to disease and uneven in size, it lost area from the 1975-84 spread of F1 varieties; about 31 Sapporo farms grow it now.
flavor: Sweet, pungent raw, sweet when cooked.
craft: High moisture and soft flesh mean short storage life. Sugar numbers come from sellers, not primary data.

name: Danshaku imo
text: Potato said to descend from Irish Cobbler brought from England in 1908 by Baron Kawada of Hakodate, which suited the Hokkaido climate and spread. Floury and fluffy.
craft: Floury texture suits mashing; it breaks down in long simmering.

name: Meequeen potato
text: Elongated oval potato with a smooth surface. It resists collapse in cooking and is introduced as suited to curry and stew. Arrived in Japan in early Showa according to one source.
craft: Holds its shape in simmering.

name: Kita Akari potato
text: Round like danshaku, with yellow flesh and reddish sprout eyes. Sweet, nicknamed kuri-jaga. Bred from danshaku and a disease-resistant variety, registered in 1987 or 1988 depending on source.
craft: Registration year differs between sources.
